messages.subject: warmup seems broken in develop
messages.subject_clean: warmup seems broken in develop
messages.body_plain:
Hi there!

I was running a ~1.5 month old cmdstan snapshot without a problem. I thought updating to the current version in develop would be a good idea. I also set stan and stan-math to the most recent develop versions (cmdstan refers to older git submodules).

Now my models only give me crap! That is, most of the runs are incredibly fast, only few runs run at a normal speed. To me it looks as if warmup fails to do something sensible (my residual error is way too large). I have to say that some chains give me results which are ok (different seed and different chain_id).

To cross check I also checked out cmdstan with the snapshot versions as the git submodules are set currently, see below for the hashes.

Model and data can't be shared, sorry; but I am happy to try out any updates on them.

Best,
Sebastian

cmdstan submodules:
[weberse2@node13:~/libs/cmdstan] make stan-update
git submodule update --init --recursive
Submodule path 'stan': checked out 'fb1b76962cd8495812c87f0a0e0d8ab328444f34'
Submodule path 'stan/lib/stan_math': checked out 'fe69fed0c91ac1c9f022673d70d7d94c48296e38'

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Timeline on experimental use of GMO?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Timeline on experimental use of GMO?
messages.body_plain:
[cc-ed dev list]

This should've been on our dev list, but I'll answer
here just so people don't think we're ignoring
questions.

> On Jun 1, 2016, at 10:00 AM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all -
>
> We're doing some planning on scaling up our modeling, and I wanted
> to get an idea if/when there was a timeline for an alpha version of
> GMO (is that what Andrew calls the method in the EP as a way of
> life paper?)  in Stan?

No, it's max marginal likelihood, not EP.

I believe it's still a private repo in Dustin Tran's organization
on GitHub --- he's the one coding it.

I'll let Andrew and Dustin answer the rest.  But we should
move the discussion to stan-dev, as it's not user-facing yet.

- Bob

> For context, we model customer behaviour. Most of our clients are in the
> 2-70k customers range.  For training purposes we randomly
> sample these, drawing 100-500 customers' full histories, and train our models using
> HMC. The small sample size, around 20 observations per customer, is adequate
> given our models are reasonably small, with 1-200 parameters.
> After estimating, we simulate posterior predictions for all customers'
> futures. All models are tested by estimating on simulated data to
> recapture known parameters. They perform well out of sample.
>
> A couple of upcoming clients have much larger customer books
> (1-5M customers). We'd like to make use of the richer data
> by segmenting customers (say, by geography/product) and estimate
> our current models with segment-varying parameters. We're a
> business and don't really have 2-3 days to wait around between
> model runs. I've tried to recover known parameters for our models
> using ADVI without much luck (more a function of our models
> than ADVI I suspect).
>
> One approach that I'm partial to is to
>
> 1. Estimate a pooled model on a random subset of the data.
> 2. Segment the full data, split it, and estimate the pooled
> model on each segment taking group-level parameters from
> (1) as priors.
>
> This would scale pretty easily, and I can continue using HMC,
> which I trust. As to whether my intuition is off about using priors
> in stage (2) here, I have no idea. The aim is to get something
> approximating a partial pooling model.
>
> But this is all to say that if there is a method that a) I know can recover
> known parameters,

> b) I can parallelize, and c) runs quickly,
> we'd be be happy to collaborate during experimentation phase.
>
> Jim
>

messages.body_plain:
Bob,
I think it works ok here because your prior on the hyper-variance excludes zero.  At least in the 8-schools example, the problem all comes in the neighborhood where the hyper-variance is close to 0.
A

> On Jun 1, 2016, at 3:03 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I ran the funnel in JAGS to follow along Daniel's section
> in our course.
>
>  model {
>    for (n in 1:9) { x[n] ~ dnorm(0, 1 / exp(y / 2)^2) }
>    y ~ dnorm(0, 1/3^2)

It may exclude 0 because it's on the log scale, but JAGS gets

a package installer for JAGS and then rjags just finds it on
install, then R2jags is easy to install on top of that --- took
about 2 minutes total).  But I forgot just how clunky those
R2WinBUGS and R2jags interfaces were.

slower than HMC).  I’m guessing that you’d see a lighter tail in the
Gibbs samples, but perhaps not much.

real foo(real [] a, real x);

and am having all kinds of problems.

I have implemented

inline double
foo(const std::vector<double>&a, const double& x);

in stan/math/prim/arr/fun/ . And in stan/math/rev/arr/fun I think I have implemented

inline var
foo(const std::vector<var>&a, const double& x);

by inheriting from the op_vector_vari class, even though it seems like it should inherit from the non-existent op_vector_vd_vari class. But to do that, I have to stuff x into a private member of the class in order to implement chain().

But I don't know if that actually works because it won't compile

foo(value_of<std::vector<double> >(a), x)

in order to evaluate the function. It says

error: no matching function for call to 'value_of'
                         value_of<std::vector<double> >(a),
                         ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
./stan/math/prim/scal/fun/value_of.hpp:24:19: note: candidate function [with T = std::__1::vector<double, std::__1::allocator<double> >] not viable: no known conversion from
      'vector<stan::math::var, allocator<stan::math::var>>' to 'const vector<double, allocator<double>>' for 1st argument
    inline double value_of(const T x) {
                  ^
./stan/math/prim/arr/fun/value_of.hpp:22:5: note: candidate function [with T = std::__1::vector<double, std::__1::allocator<double> >] not viable: no known conversion from
      'vector<stan::math::var>' to 'const vector<std::__1::vector<double, std::__1::allocator<double> >>' for 1st argument
    value_of(const std::vector<T>& x) {
    ^
1 error generated.

Conversely, I think I have implemented

inline var
foo(const std::vector<double>&a, const var& x);

by inheriting from the op_v_vari class after stuffing part of a into a private member of the class in order to implement chain() but it seems like there should be an op_vector_dv_vari class.

And I can't find any class to inherit from in order to implement

inline var
foo(const std::vector<var>&a, const var& x);

Ben

> On Jun 4, 2016, at 4:30 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am trying to implement C++ functions, which if written in the Stan language would have the signature
>
> real foo(real [] a, real x);
>
> and am having all kinds of problems.
>
> I have implemented
>
> inline double
> foo(const std::vector<double>&a, const double& x);
>
> in stan/math/prim/arr/fun/ .

OK, this is right.

> And in stan/math/rev/arr/fun I think I have implemented
>
> inline var
> foo(const std::vector<var>&a, const double& x);

First off, you don't want to use double references --- just direct
calls (the const doesn't change the API because it's pass-by value).
So that's:

  (const vector<var>&, double) : var

  (const vector<double>&, var) : var

  (const vector<var>&, var) : var

> by inheriting from the op_vector_vari class, even though it seems like it should inherit from the non-existent op_vector_vd_vari class.

You can write that op_vector_vd_vari class.  You can
even extend op_vector_vari to do it.

> But to do that, I have to stuff x into a private member of the class in order to implement chain().

Right --- that'd be how to do the general extension, too.

> But I don't know if that actually works because it won't compile
>
> foo(value_of<std::vector<double> >(a), x)

Where is that call coming from?  You shouldn't need to use value_of
anywhere --- we use it in the density functions in order to
pull out the double-based values from containers in order to
do generic vectorization.  And I believe it's only defined for scalars,
so you'd have to use a loop.

If you do want to call it, you'll need to include the appropriate
definitions.  The way math is set up is that dependencies look like this:

   scalar <- array <- matrix

   double <- rev <- mix
          <- fwd <---|

Where "array" is Stan arrays, meaning std::vector.

> in order to evaluate the function. It says
>
> error: no matching function for call to 'value_of'
>                          value_of<std::vector<double> >(a),
>                          ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
> ./stan/math/prim/scal/fun/value_of.hpp:24:19: note: candidate function [with T = std::__1::vector<double, std::__1::allocator<double> >] not viable: no known conversion from
>       'vector<stan::math::var, allocator<stan::math::var>>' to 'const vector<double, allocator<double>>' for 1st argument
>     inline double value_of(const T x) {
>                   ^

This is just saying that it's only defined for var arguments, not double
arguments.

> ./stan/math/prim/arr/fun/value_of.hpp:22:5: note: candidate function [with T = std::__1::vector<double, std::__1::allocator<double> >] not viable: no known conversion from
>       'vector<stan::math::var>' to 'const vector<std::__1::vector<double, std::__1::allocator<double> >>' for 1st argument
>     value_of(const std::vector<T>& x) {
>     ^
> 1 error generated.

this on'e snot relevant as it's vector<vector<T> >.

> Conversely, I think I have implemented
>
> inline var
> foo(const std::vector<double>&a, const var& x);
>
> by inheriting from the op_v_vari class after stuffing part of a into a private member of the class in order to implement chain() but it seems like there should be an op_vector_dv_vari class.
>
> And I can't find any class to inherit from in order to implement
>
> inline var
> foo(const std::vector<var>&a, const var& x);

Right --- you're going to have to write your own base classes
for this.  As far as I know, we don't have any signatures that
apply to a mix of scalar and std::vector --- all of those functions
use Eigen types.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
We haven’t established any convention.  I’ve tried to make all of my
implementations accurate as close to machine precision as possible
with exceptions thrown in case any loops exceed some very large,
preset value.  Technically trying to treat numerical issues with
exceptions (and hence a Metropolis rejection) can bias the Markov
chain, but I haven’t seen any of these exceptions thrown in
production code (or at least not after improving implementations).

I still occasionally get numerical exceptions with

Derivatives aren't really any different here, are they?

Is there something you'd suggest rather than rejecting?
I'm not even sure at this point if this just counts as
a U-turn or whether it rejects the whole tree being built.

We need to refactor our exception types to make them follow
something like this:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_61_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/error_handling.html

For now, you can just throw a std::domain_error, which we throw
all over the place when we should probably be throwing a std::range_error
for these situations:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/22978863/differences-between-out-of-range-range-error-and-over-underflow-error

It only matters for users of the Math library --- the exceptions
all work the same way in Stan as long as they inherit from std::exception.

messages.subject: Evaluating mean-field ADVI: 1. Some results
messages.subject_clean: Evaluating mean-field ADVI: 1. Some results
messages.body_plain:
Hi--as many of you know, Rayleigh wrote a script based on some code of Ben to run NUTS and then mean-field ADVI on a library of over 200 Stan programs (the Bugs examples, the Arm examples, and a bunch more:  https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/wiki).  The idea, for each  model, was to first run NUTS to convergence, and then run ADVI to check that the estimates from ADVI were close.  To give ADVI the best chance of succeeding, we used the posterior mean estimates from NUTS as our starting points for ADVI.

Next it's time to summarize the evaluations.  For each parameter in a model, we define "close" in terms of the z-score:  ((ADVI estimate) - (posterior mean))/(posterior sd), where the posterior mean and sd are from NUTS.  The idea is that this z-score should be close to zero.  For each model, we computed the maximum of the z-scores for all the parameters in the model (which includes transformed parameters and generated quantities).  We then had 200-plus max z-scores, which we plotted; see attached.

messages.subject: Evaluating mean-field ADVI: 2. Data and code
messages.subject_clean: Evaluating mean-field ADVI: 2. Data and code
messages.body_plain:
So, I ran Rayleigh's script which runs mean-field ADVI on 234 existing Stan models and compares the results to NUTS (which had already been fit on these models).  The workflow goes like this:

clean_NUTS_info.Rdata:  This file contains the results of the previous NUTS runs for all the models.  For each model, NUTS was run to convergence and we saved the posterior mean and posterior sd of each parameter.

advi_test.R:  This script runs meanfield ADVI on each model.  For about 39 of the models, ADVI failed in that it did not give answers at all; for the others it gives parameter estimates, which we save in ADVI_report_info.Rdata and ADVI_report_info.csv.

ADVI_report_info.Rdata, a file that includes the NUTS results from clean_NUTS_info.Rdata and also the new ADVI results.

ADVI_report_info.csv:  For convenience, the same thing in a huge (104 MB) .csv file.

advi_test_explore.R:  A script I wrote to explore the results and compare ADVI to NUTS.

We'd particularly like to understand under what conditions
ADVI has a hard time recovering model parameters that HMC
can recover.  It'd be great to do better overall.  Figuring
out why some models don't work at all would be a good
start.  I'd be very happy if we could find a well-behaved
class of models.  Or even a combination of model parameters
and models.  For example, if we do a good job on the individual-level
parameters but not the hierarchical parameters in a multilevel
model, that'd still be very useful.

> Some thoughts:
>
> + ADVI didn’t do as bad as I thought! :)

Were your expectations low because of data sizes or some
features of the model and the Gaussian approximation?

> + The current scenario is not technically the most ideal. The ideal for ADVI is not only to initialize at NUTS’ posterior mean estimate but also the NUTS' posterior sd estimates. That is, the normal variational distribution has good inits for its mean parameter but not its standard deviation parameter. To do this ideal scenario first is an interfacing issue with Stan, i.e., it is the question of how to initialize both parameters in ADVI, most likely in the unconstrained space. (This is also relevant to GMO, and why I had to give up on VI-based experiments in the R package and re-implement GMO+ADVI+Laplace in Edward).

We can retrieve the posterior sd, so it's only a matter of initializing ADVI.
The new interfaces Daniel's working on should make this kind of
change much easier going forward (and easier to propagate to all
the interfaces).

What I've been hoping is that ADVI could get us to the typical set
quickly from which we can then do relatively fast adaptation and thus
be able to spread MCMC around multiple cores for scalability of
actual draws.  But if it takes each core a long time to warmup, or
there's a big up front lag, then the overall time saved by parallelization
is severely limited.

> + the ARMS earnings model: Yep it’s an issue with the posterior standard deviations. The mean-field sd is very off on the a1’s and a2’s. This is okay for the parameters we directly infer, because the evaluation metric does not account for their sd estimates. But for inferring induced distributions that ultimately use the variance, the evaluation metric will spot them. So as you said, this suggests splitting the evaluation metric into two pieces, because the current metric is spotting two different problems: (a) check how ADVI estimates posterior means only on the parameters it directly infers, and no induced distributions; (b) check how ADVI estimates posterior sd on the parameters it directly infers, and no induced distributions

I don't understand what you mean by "directly infer" and "induced
distribution".  Don't you estimate all the parameters (and derived
quantities) declared in the model?

- Bob

Progress writer: key-value with log level for progress messages, respects log4j log levels
Output writer: csv-style output file, estimates and related diagnostic quantities
Diagnostic writer: csv-style diagnostic file, internal versions of parameters and related diagnostic quantities, potentially respects log4j log levels

If anyone has comments at this stage let me know.

Krzysztof

the linked packages that don't automatically include CVODES.

math-cvodes.hpp.

Managing dependencies is always a burden, which is why I'm so
conservative in wanting to add them to Stan.

messages.subject: FYI: new git 2.9 feature, --shallow-submodules
messages.subject_clean: FYI: new git 2.9 feature, --shallow-submodules
messages.body_plain:
There's a new feature in git 2.9 which looks like it might be useful for
speeding up some CI tests:

Source: https://blog.bitbucket.org/2016/06/13/git-2-9/

> git clone learned −−shallow-submodules
>
> If you’re using submodules, you’re in luck – for once! 🙂 Git 2.9
> introduces the −−shallow-submodules flag that allows you to grab a
> full clone of your repository, and then recursively shallow clone any
> referenced submodules to a depth of one commit. This is useful if you
> don’t need the full history of your project’s dependencies. For
> example, if you have a large monorepo with each project stored as a
> submodule, you may want to clone with shallow submodules initially,
> and then selectively deepen the few projects you want to work with.
> Another scenario would be configuring a CI or CD job that needs to
> perform a merge: Git needs the primary repository’s history in order
> to perform its recursive merge algorithm, and you’ll likely also need
> the latest commit from each of your submodules in order to actually
> perform the build. However you probably don’t need the full history
> for every submodule, so retrieving just the latest commit will save
> you both time and bandwidth.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the inventory of what's going on now.  That's
very helpful.

As to goal, I don't think there needs to be a consolidated
output format for MCMC, MLE, and VB (or diagnostics) in the
sense that each produces output mutually readable by the other.

What I do think we want is a way to round trip all of
the following in a modular reader/writer fashion:

1) single parameter values

2) sequences of parameter values, perhaps named
   (e.g., MCMC init value vs. draws; VB init vs. draws vs.
    best fit)

3) vectors and matrices (if we don't want to make this
   just an instance of parameter values)

4) key-value pairs for config information (I see that you're
   structuring keys rather than allowing values to have
   structure --- just pointing that out, I can see arguments
   either way)

5) specific relevalnt types, like time

It would be possible to put all this together into
some kind of structure if we can stream it all out in
a reasonable way.

I think that's what's being targeted in the "BIG DESIGN DECISION"
section, but I'm not sure.

There are some nitpicky little details here and there.  The timing
estimate, for example, isn't really part of the config for HMC.
Nor are the adapted step size or mass matrix, though you'd need to
save those if you wanted to restart.  So what we need is a step size
(or integration time) and mass matrix;  you already have the former
but we need to generalize to the latter in Stan 3.

We don't need to build all of these on top of a base writer.
So I'd be more inclined to have progress writer (or other loggers)
have methods .warn(), .error(), .info(), etc than have
it use key-values with keys defined.  For one things, keys are
very slow.  We also need an .if_warn(), ..., and so forth, so we
can check what level the logger's at so we can avoid constructing
messages that will get swallowed.

I like the "sample writer" abstraction --- that's what I was talking
about above.  Then we'd replace the current CSV reader thing with
something that modularly actually used a proper CSV reader (that is, one
that only reads CSV files and ignores comment lines, not one that
requires specific comment content).

- Bob

unique output source for each verbosity level and all messages are just
passed to the appropriate source)?

> be

> output source and a desired verbosity and all messages at that verbosity
> or lower are passed to the output source)
>
> or
>
> (2) unique output sources (any implementation would define a potentially
> unique output source for each verbosity level and all messages are just
> passed to the appropriate source)?

Usually, you have something like a filter pattern that you
wrap around loggers to produce new loggers.  Some of them
turn off output, some tee it to multiple sources.  So if you
had logger1 and logger2, you might have tee(logger1, logger2)
as a new logger implementing the same logging interface, or
filter_warn(logger1) if you don't go below warnings.

But then that's all usually wrapped up with file config for input
and output sources that are put together with reflection.

I don't think we need to get this crazy---just having the
right interface for logging is the way to start.  And maybe an
output format.

- Bob

> wrap around loggers to produce new loggers.  Some of them

> and output sources that are put together with reflection.
>
> I don't think we need to get this crazy---just having the

> output format.
>

messages.body_plain:
Most of these are going to have to be built into the parser
code itself to do it right, especially given the creative
syntax we see from users.

I don't know if the "sigma..." thing is worth doing.  Not
many of our users use "sigma" or "sigma_foo" the way Andrew does.  And
presumably you meant should have <lower=0> in its declaration?
It probably got lost in the markdown.

Do we also flag normal(0, 1000) and other attempts at very
diffuse priors?

The problem with a lot of this is that we'll have to be
doing simple blind matching.  Most of our users don't
use "sigma" (or "tau" the way Andrew does).  Nor do they
follow the sigma_foo standard---it's all over the place.

We can pick up literal values (and by literal, I mean
it's a number in the code).  We won't be able to pick up
more complex things like gamma(a, b) where a < 1 and b < 1,
because that's a run-time issue, not a compile-time issue,
for instance if a and b are data.

Should we also flag <lower=A> if A != 0 or A!= -1?   (Again,
we'll be able to pick up literal numbers there, not more
complex violations).

Conditionals (if-else) are only problematic if the conditions
depend on parameters.

Everyone wants to do more complicated things, like make sure
that if a variable is given a distribution with a bound that the
bound's declared in the parameters.  So no:

  real alpha;

  alpha ~ lognormal(...)

because then alpha isn't well defined. These things are going to
be a lot of work to track down and we'll again only be able to pick
out direct cases like this.

- Bob

I was thinking the logger is an object instance
and there's just one, but you can send messages

The trick in all the frameworks is making the logger
available programatically without having to pass it
around everywhere.  But I think we can just pass ours
around like the writers.  Otherwise, it's going to need

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output progress
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] output progress
messages.body_plain:
Implementing ostream would be nice, but that's
trickier.  I'd start with just this interface:

class logger {
   // set level (all messages at level or above printed)
   void set_debug();
   void set_warn();
   void set_error();

   // query what level is set
   bool is_debug() const;
   bool is_warn() const;
   bool is_error() const;

   // log a message
   void debug(const string& msg);
   void warn(const string& msg);
   void error(const string& msg);
}

and maybe some additional levels.

If you want to get fancy, then it'd be something like this:

  ostream& debug();
  ostream& warn();
  ostream& error();

That'd be a much cleaner interface in C++, but then you need
to have no-op streams if the level's above the logger requested.

You want the "is_debug()" or something like it to avoid
constructing big strings that are then just thrown away,
especially at lower levels of granularity like debug.

- Bob

and use.

the fly, things could get very ugly (in the code) very fast,
as the underlying parser's just a huge pain to work with.

> On Jun 22, 2016, at 1:03 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> So what’s the best place to introduce these checks?
> It’s not dissimilar for what’s already done with the
> Jacobian checks, no?

It depends what they are.  I should've been clearer that
I meant on the fly as in find the issue as it's parsing.

There are two approaches --- plumb enough information top
down through the parser so that we can check inside of
a single expression or statement --- that's what the Jacobian
check does now.  To do that, the source of every variable
needs to be plumbed through the entire parse tree.  If we do
more of that it's going to get ugly.  Some of these are
"peephole" warnings --- things you can catch just locally.

For others, we have the AST and can design walkers for it
that walk over the code any old way and report.

Or, we could do something hacky with regexes along the
lines of cpplint (a Python program, not something plumbed into
the C++ parser, at least as far as I know).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output progress
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] output progress
messages.body_plain:
It's easy to go both ways.  With a stringstream, you can
just collect output into a buffer, so it's easy to produce
output streams.  With an output stream, it's easy to feed
it strings.  Just a matter of whether it's worth the extra
work.

- Bob

> On Jun 22, 2016, at 1:02 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> No-op streams are straightforward to implement
> so that’s not an issue.  The question is whether or
> not the interfaces can actually produce a stream
> easily (i.e. if it’s much easier for them to accept
> strings).
>
> On Jun 22, 2016, at 9:24 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> Implementing ostream would be nice, but that's
>> trickier.  I'd start with just this interface:
>>
>> class logger {
>>  // set level (all messages at level or above printed)
>>  void set_debug();
>>  void set_warn();
>>  void set_error();
>>
>>  // query what level is set
>>  bool is_debug() const;
>>  bool is_warn() const;
>>  bool is_error() const;
>>
>>  // log a message
>>  void debug(const string& msg);
>>  void warn(const string& msg);
>>  void error(const string& msg);
>> }
>>
>> and maybe some additional levels.
>>
>> If you want to get fancy, then it'd be something like this:
>>
>> ostream& debug();
>> ostream& warn();
>> ostream& error();
>>
>> That'd be a much cleaner interface in C++, but then you need
>> to have no-op streams if the level's above the logger requested.
>>
>> You want the "is_debug()" or something like it to avoid
>> constructing big strings that are then just thrown away,
>> especially at lower levels of granularity like debug.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>>> On Jun 22, 2016, at 12:05 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> Yes, that would be the basic interface.  But how
>>> should that be implemented?  Does the base
>>> code pass in strings which are filtered by the
>>> logger and _then_ passed to whatever sources
>>> the interfaces provide?  Or do the interfaces
>>> provide a source for each level, and the logger
>>> just passes strings to the appropriate source?
>>>
>>> And do we want to pass strings or char arrays
>>> or do the interfaces provide ostreams to which
>>> various objects are dumped?
>>>
>>> On Jun 22, 2016, at 8:56 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>>> I'm afraid I don't understand the question.
>>>>
>>>> I was thinking the logger is an object instance
>>>> and there's just one, but you can send messages
>>>> to it at various log levels and then it can be
>>>> filtered to only print messages above a certain
>>>> severity.  Basically, just another kind of writer.
>>>>
>>>> The trick in all the frameworks is making the logger
>>>> available programatically without having to pass it
>>>> around everywhere.  But I think we can just pass ours
>>>> around like the writers.  Otherwise, it's going to need
>>>> to be global like the memory for the autodiff.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
>>>>
>>>>
>>>>> On Jun 21, 2016, at 5:08 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>> Sure — my question was really an implementation one.
>>>>> In particular, do the interfaces want a bunch of parallel
>>>>> sources or one source that gets filtered by the logger
>>>>> itself.
>>>>>
>>>>> On Jun 21, 2016, at 6:47 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>>>
>>>>>>> On Jun 21, 2016, at 9:51 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> On Jun 21, 2016, at 3:22 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> I think we already had one go-around on this with Michael that came down
>>>>>>>> to a good interface:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> 1) https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Logging-Spec
>>>>>>>> 2) https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-dev/Betancourt%7Csort:date/stan-dev/YJvyzVTK_YQ/fzNhwbg4BgAJ
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> I'm guessing what you want is a spec that outlines the signatures for the calls
>>>>>>>> to the loggers?  I can do that on the wiki and go from there.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> Let’s separate out the logger from file/environment I/O.  That way the logger
>>>>>>> can be implemented and merged quickly and avoid most of the design issues.
>>>>>>> It’s been on my todo list, but so has a million other things.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> I do have one last question regarding the logger: do we want the levels to
>>>>>>> be
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> (1) a threshold for a single output (any implementation would define an
>>>>>>> output source and a desired verbosity and all messages at that verbosity
>>>>>>> or lower are passed to the output source)
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> or
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> (2) unique output sources (any implementation would define a potentially
>>>>>>> unique output source for each verbosity level and all messages are just
>>>>>>> passed to the appropriate source)?
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Usually, you have something like a filter pattern that you
>>>>>> wrap around loggers to produce new loggers.  Some of them
>>>>>> turn off output, some tee it to multiple sources.  So if you
>>>>>> had logger1 and logger2, you might have tee(logger1, logger2)
>>>>>> as a new logger implementing the same logging interface, or
>>>>>> filter_warn(logger1) if you don't go below warnings.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> But then that's all usually wrapped up with file config for input
>>>>>> and output sources that are put together with reflection.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I don't think we need to get this crazy---just having the
>>>>>> right interface for logging is the way to start.  And maybe an
>>>>>> output format.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> - Bob

messages.subject: CmdStan v2.10.0 released!
messages.subject_clean: CmdStan v2.10.0 released!
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

CmdStan v2.10.0 has been released: https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/tag/v2.10.0

Most of the changes in CmdStan are due to improvements in the Stan library. Below are the user-facing changes in Stan v2.10.0. For more information, see the full release notes for Stan: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/tag/v2.10.0

New User-Facing Features
--------------------------------------------------
* introduction of = for assignment; deprecating <- (#1819)
* _lpdf, _lpmf, _lcdf, _lccdf and vertical bar notation
  for probability mass, density, and cumulative distribution
  functions; update user-defined function syntax;
  deprecate older forms (#1811)
* target += lp to replace increment_log_prob(lp); target() to rpelace
  log_prob() function;  remove lp__ variable access (#1800)
* conditional (ternary) operator (#1125)
* stiff diff eq solver CVODES from Sundials
* add control parameters (tolerance, max iteraitons) to ODE solvers
* rename ODE solvers based on algorithm, integrate_ode_rk45
  for existing non-stiff Runge-Kutta solver and integrate_ode_bdf
  for the stiff backward differentiation form;  deprecate
  the unmarked integrate_ode function (#1886)
* limiting diff eq iterations in solvers (Boost/CVODES)
* unit_vector as parameter (#1713) [it never worked in the past]
* rename multiply_log and log_binomial_coefficient
  to lmultiply and lchoose (also part of #1811)
* incomplete beta function as inc_beta (#1540)

Daniel

P.S. Rob, please start testing with this version. If there are any issues, please let me know.

> Is there a way I can reproduce this locally? Or possibly log into a machine that has it set up?

You can pull all of the rstan repo, including the submodules in StanHeaders/inst/include and then do

R CMD build StanHeaders
R CMD INSTALL StanHeaders_2.10.0-2.tar.gz
R CMD build rstan/rstan
R CMD INSTALL rstan_2.10.1.tar.gz

I fixed it by changing rstan/rstan/src/Makevars to define BOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1_WITH_DECLTYPE_FALLBACK rather than -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE but that doesn't work under the pre-C++11 standard, so now it is using C++11 on everything but Windows and leaving -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE instead of -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1_WITH_DECLTYPE_FALLBACK on Windows.

Ben

We want to be able to do this anyway for our other warnings.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] I added to the pedantic mode page
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] I added to the pedantic mode page
messages.body_plain:
I was thinking of “pedantic” as in the pedantic C++
compiler option, hence my thinking of it being done
in the parser.  An added benefit of this approach is
that it would allow us to turn it on by default and force
users to turn it off.

But a lint-like system would be good, too.

> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] I added to the pedantic mode page
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] I added to the pedantic mode page
messages.body_plain:
Yup --- that's what I understood you to mean.
That'd be things like not defining variables before
they're used and not having constraints on parameters
used in uniform distributions and the like.

Crossing over into style, like which priors to
use and whether to include spaces, passes into lint
territory.   Arguably the Jacobian warnings are also
in this category in that they're not ill-formed
programs, they just might not do what the user expects.

- Bob

messages.subject: refactor coupled_ode_system
messages.subject_clean: refactor coupled_ode_system
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

As mentioned during the meeting, I would like to refactor the coupled_ode_system with the goal

- to get stiff and non-stiff ODE stuff aligned in the way they are implemented for easier maintenance

- make both (stiff+non-stiff) use the ode_system object introduced with CVODES patches

- this will enable to provide analytic Jacobians via partial template specialization to the stiff and non-stiff system at the same time

I started a branch here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor

and the respective issue is this one:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/310

The implementation follows very closely the design of CVODES stuff, so I hope things are in a good state already. At this stage I was able to cut down the code by 500 lines, but lets wait for the review...

I suggest to do discussions on the issue unless we need a longer design phase, then we are probably better off with a wiki page.

>From my end my only question would be if I should also remove the decouple_states function from the coupled_ode_system object. The decoupling operation could easily be moved into the integrate_ode_rk45 function (using the decouple_ode_states function).

If someone of the "ODE-code-exposed" persons could look into this, that would be great. Don't be scared by the many files moved around, this is only due to the fact that tests needed to relocate. The center-piece of the patch is in stan/math/rev/mat/functor/coupled_ode_system.hpp .

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian
